subject: physics
title: Line Spectra and Energy Level Transitions
welcome_lead: Decode an atomic fingerprint by reading bright emission and dark absorption lines.
meta_desc: A-Level Quantum Phenomena adventure on emission, absorption and energy level transitions.
final_note: Each element has unique line spectra — fingerprints written by quantum mechanics.

concepts.def: All wavelengths, from hot solid/dense gas.

walkthroughs.body_html: Hot, low-density gas: atoms excite, then drop down, emitting photons at specific energies. Spectrum shows bright lines at those wavelengths.
Cool gas in front of continuous source: photons matching transition energies are absorbed. Dark Fraunhofer lines appear in otherwise continuous spectrum.
Transitions ending at n=1 are Lyman (UV), at n=2 Balmer (visible), at n=3 Paschen (IR). Each gives a fixed set of wavelengths from hf = E₂ − E₁.

mcqs.q: The Balmer series transitions end at:
Why do atoms emit light only at specific wavelengths rather than a continuous spectrum?
options: Atoms can emit any wavelength, but only certain ones are visible.
Intensity has no effect on anything in the photoelectric effect.
Atoms emit only one colour each, determined by their temperature.
Electrons occupy discrete energy levels; transitions between levels emit photons of specific frequencies (E = hf).

mcqs.q: What determines the energy of a single photon?
options: A brighter light has higher-energy photons because intensity makes each photon more energetic.
Its frequency (E = hf) — only frequency, not intensity.
Photon energy depends on how fast the photon is moving relative to the source.
Intensity has no effect on anything in the photoelectric effect.

mcqs.q: How does the maximum kinetic energy of photoelectrons depend on light intensity?
options: It does not — max KE depends only on the frequency of the light; intensity affects the rate (number) of electrons emitted.
Higher intensity gives photoelectrons more kinetic energy.
Photon energy depends on how fast the photon is moving relative to the source.
Intensity has no effect on anything in the photoelectric effect.
